title: Landlord's obligation to maintain premises
text: 83.51 Landlord's obligation to maintain premises.— (1) The landlord at all times during the tenancy shall: (a) Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes; or (b) Where there are no applicable building, housing, or health codes, maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition. (2)(a) Unless otherwise agreed in writing, in addition to the requirements of subsection (1), the landlord of a dwelling unit other than a single-family home or duplex shall, at all times during the tenancy, make reasonable provisions for: 1. The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs. 2. Locks and keys. 3. The clean and safe condition of common areas. 4. Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor. 5. Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water.
summary: Specifies a landlord's duty to maintain a rental property. This includes complying with all health and building codes, and ensuring structural components are in good repair. For multi-family units, the landlord must also reasonably provide for pest control, locks, clean common areas, garbage removal, and functioning heat and water facilities.

title: Termination of rental agreement
text: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement.— (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51(1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51(1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties...
summary: Allows a tenant to terminate a lease if the landlord materially fails to comply with their duty to maintain the premises (per § 83.51) or the lease agreement. The tenant must give 7 days' written notice. If the landlord's failure is due to circumstances beyond their control but they are making reasonable efforts to fix the issue, the lease may be altered or terminated by agreement.

title: Legislative findings and declaration
text: 558.001 Legislative findings and declaration.—The Legislature finds that it is beneficial to have an alternative method to resolve construction disputes that would reduce the need for litigation as well as protect the rights of property owners. An effective alternative dispute resolution mechanism in certain construction defect matters should involve the claimant filing a notice of claim with the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional that the claimant asserts is responsible for the defect, and should provide the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional, and the insurer of the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional, with an opportunity to resolve the claim through confidential settlement negotiations without resort to further legal process.
summary: Establishes legislative purpose of Chapter 558 to provide alternative dispute resolution for construction defects through pre-litigation notice and settlement procedures, protecting property owners while reducing litigation burden.

title: Definitions
text: 558.002 Definitions.—As used in this chapter, the term: (1) "Action" means any civil action or arbitration proceeding for damages or indemnity asserting a claim for damage to or loss of real or personal property caused by an alleged construction defect, but does not include any administrative action or any civil action or arbitration proceeding asserting a claim for alleged personal injuries arising out of an alleged construction defect. (2) "Association" has the same meaning as in s. 718.103, s. 719.103(2), s. 720.301(9),. (3) "Claimant" means a property owner, including a subsequent purchaser or association, who asserts a claim for damages against a contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional concerning a construction defect. The term does not include a contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional. (4) "Completion of a building or improvement" means issuance of a certificate of occupancy. (5) "Construction defect" means a deficiency in, or a deficiency arising out of, the design, specifications, surveying, planning, supervision, observation of construction, or construction, repair, alteration, or remodeling of real property resulting from: (a) Defective material, products, or components used in the construction or remodeling; (b) A violation of the applicable codes in effect at the time of construction or remodeling which gives rise to a cause of action pursuant to s. 553.84; (c) A failure of the design of real property to meet the applicable professional standards of care at the time of governmental approval; or (d) A failure to construct or remodel real property in accordance with accepted trade standards for good and workmanlike construction at the time of construction.
summary: Defines key terms for Chapter 558 including construction defect (deficiencies from defective materials, code violations, design failures, or failure to meet workmanship standards), claimant (property owners/associations excluding contractors), and service requirements.

excerpts.label: Construction defect definition
excerpts.text: Construction defect means a deficiency arising from: (a) Defective material, products, or components; (b) Code violations; (c) Failure of design to meet professional standards; or (d) Failure to construct in accordance with accepted trade standards.

notes: History: s. 2, ch. 2003-49; most recent s. 18, ch. 2023-203

title: Definitions
text: 713.01 Definitions.—As used in this part, the term: (1) 'Direct contract' means a contract between an owner and a contractor that provides for the labor, services, or materials furnished in connection with the improvement of real property. (2) 'Improvement' means the alteration, addition to, repair, demolition, or construction of real property; the clearing, filling, or excavating of land; or the planting or removal of trees, shrubs, or plants on real property. (3) 'Labor' means work or labor done upon the real property. (4) 'Lienor' means a person entitled to claim a lien under this part. (5) 'Materials' means all materials, machinery, fixtures, or tools, including specifically power-driven construction equipment, which are used or rented upon real property in connection with the construction, alteration, or repair thereof. (6) 'Owner' means the person who has an interest in the real property improved and for whose benefit the improvement is made. (7) 'Real property' means land and includes all tenements, hereditaments, and improvements thereon.
summary: Defines key terms for Chapter 713 mechanic's liens including direct contract, improvement, labor, lienor, materials, owner, and real property. Establishes foundational definitions for liens on real property for labor, services, or materials provided for improvements.

title: Extent of lien
text: 713.06 Extent of lien.—(1) All mechanics' liens, except those arising by virtue of a direct contract with the owner, shall be subject to the limitations of this section. (2) No lien shall exceed the amount of the contract price between the owner and the direct contractor. (3) A lien based upon a contract for less than the reasonable value of the services or materials is to the extent of such reasonable value, as provided in s. 713.05, effective and prior to a mortgage or other lien not otherwise preferred attaching prior to the commencement of the improvement. A lien based on a contract is to the extent of the contract price effective and prior to a mortgage or other lien not otherwise preferred attaching prior to the commencement of the improvement.
summary: Establishes the extent and limitations of mechanic's liens in Florida. Generally, liens cannot exceed the owner's contract price with the direct contractor. Liens based on reasonable value or contract price have priority over mortgages that attach before improvement commences.

title: Time for recording claim of lien
text: 713.13 Time for recording claim of lien.—(1) Any lienor may preserve and protect the lien given by this part by recording, within the time provided by this section, a claim of lien. (2) A contractor under a direct contract with the owner must record a claim of lien no later than 90 days after the final furnishing of the labor, services, or materials by the lienor. (3) All lienors, other than contractors under a direct contract with the owner, shall record a claim of lien no later than 90 days after the last day they performed labor or services or furnished materials. (4) For the purposes of calculating the 90-day period, if a lienor is a laborer, the last day shall be the last date the laborer performed labor regardless of whether the laborer is paid by the day, week, or month.
summary: Establishes time limits for recording mechanic's lien claims. Contractors under direct contract with owner and other lienors must record within 90 days of final furnishing of labor, services, or materials. Failure to timely record results in loss of lien rights.

title: Limitations other than for the recovery of real property
text: 95.11 Limitations other than for the recovery of real property.—Actions other than for recovery of real property shall be commenced as follows: (1) WITHIN TWENTY YEARS.—An action upon a judgment or decree of a court of record. (2) WITHIN FIVE YEARS.—(a) A legal or equitable action on a contract, obligation, or liability founded on a written instrument. (b) An action for assault, battery, false imprisonment, false arrest, malicious prosecution, malicious interference, or a statutory claim. (c) An action sounding in fraud or deceit. (d) A claim for specific performance of a contract. (e) An action for waste. (3) WITHIN FOUR YEARS.—(a) An action for injury to the person. (b) An action for injury to personal property. (c) An action for the recovery of wrongfully held personal property. (d) An action for the crime of misappropriation of trade secrets. (e) An action for specific performance for the sale of goods under s. 672.725(1). (f) An action based on the design, manufacture, or construction of an improvement to real property except as provided in subsection (4). (g) An action founded on a statutory liability other than a forfeiture or penalty. (h) An action or defense relating to the determination of any interest in property, whether legal or equitable, which action or defense is not otherwise provided for by law.
summary: Establishes limitation periods for various civil actions in Florida. Five-year limitations for written contracts, fraud, assault, battery, malicious prosecution; four-year limitations for personal injury, property injury, construction defects; two-year limitations for professional malpractice and products liability; other specific timeframes for various claims.

title: Attorney's fee; sanctions for raising unsupported claims or defenses; exceptions; service of motions; damages for delay
text: 57.105 Attorney's fee; sanctions for raising unsupported claims or defenses; exceptions; service of motions; damages for delay.—(1) Upon the court's initiative or motion of any party, the court shall award a reasonable attorney's fee, including prejudgment interest, to be paid to the prevailing party in equal amounts by the losing party and the losing party's attorney on any claim or defense at any time during a civil proceeding or action in which the court finds that the losing party or the losing party's attorney knew or should have known that a claim or defense when initially presented to the court or at any time before trial: (a) Was not supported by the material facts necessary to establish the claim or defense; or (b) Would not be supported by the application of then-existing law to those material facts. (3) At any time in any civil proceeding or action in which the moving party proves by a preponderance of the evidence that any action taken by the opposing party, including, but not limited to, the filing of any pleading or part thereof, the assertion of or response to any discovery demand, the assertion of any claim or defense, or the response to any request by any other party, was taken primarily for the purpose of unreasonable delay, the court shall award damages to the moving party for its reasonable expenses incurred in obtaining the order.
summary: Authorizes courts to award attorney's fees and sanctions against a party or attorney who raises unsupported claims or defenses that are not grounded in material facts or applicable law. Also provides for damages when a party acts primarily to cause unreasonable delay. Includes safe harbor provision requiring 21-day notice before filing.

title: Unlawful acts and practices
text: 501.204 Unlawful acts and practices.—(1) Unfair methods of competition, unconscionable acts or practices, and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce are hereby declared unlawful. (2) It is the intent of the Legislature that, in construing subsection (1), the courts shall be guided by the Federal Trade Commission Act, 15 U.S.C. §§ 41-58, and the interpretations thereof by the Federal Trade Commission and the federal courts. (3) For purposes of this part, a person engages in a deceptive and unfair trade practice when, in the course of the person's business or occupation, the person: (a) Represents that a subject of a consumer transaction has sponsorship, approval, performance characteristics, accessories, uses, or benefits that it does not have. (b) Represents that a subject of a consumer transaction is of a particular standard, quality, grade, style, or model that it is not. (c) Disparages the goods, services, or business of another by false or misleading representations of fact. (d) Advertises goods, services, or property with intent not to sell them as advertised, or with intent not to sell at the price or upon the terms advertised. (e) Makes false or misleading statements of fact concerning the reasons for, existence of, or amounts of price reductions.
summary: FDUTPA's core prohibition making unfair, deceptive, or unconscionable trade practices unlawful in Florida. Courts interpret this statute guided by Federal Trade Commission Act precedent. Specific unlawful practices include false representations about product characteristics, quality, advertising with no intent to sell, deceptive pricing, and disparagement of competitors.

title: Remedies; civil actions
text: 501.211 Remedies; civil actions.—(1) A person who has suffered a loss as a result of a violation of this part may bring a civil action to obtain: (a) A declaratory judgment that an act or practice violates this part; (b) An injunction; (c) Recovery of actual damages; and (d) Court costs and reasonable attorney fees. (2) In addition to the recovery under subsection (1), the court may assess civil penalties in an amount not to exceed $10,000 for each violation of this part if the court finds: (a) The defendant willfully engaged in a deceptive or unfair trade practice; or (b) The defendant engaged in a deceptive or unfair trade practice that was part of a pattern or practice of such conduct. (3) The prevailing plaintiff in a civil action brought under this section shall be awarded a reasonable attorney's fee and court costs.
summary: Establishes private right of action under FDUTPA. Consumers harmed by unfair or deceptive practices may sue for declaratory judgment, injunction, actual damages, attorney fees, and costs. Courts may also assess civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation for willful or pattern conduct. Prevailing plaintiffs are awarded attorney fees.

title: Definitions
text: 83.43 Definitions.—As used in this part, the following words and terms shall have the following meanings, unless some other meaning is plainly indicated: (1) 'Dwelling unit' means: (a) A structure or part of a structure that is rented for use as a home, residence, or sleeping place by one person or by two or more persons who maintain a common household. (b) A mobile home rented by a tenant. (c) A structure or part of a structure that is furnished, with or without rent, as an incident of employment for use as a home, residence, or sleeping place by one or more persons. (2) 'Landlord' means the owner or lessor of a dwelling unit. (3) 'Tenant' means any person entitled to occupy a dwelling unit under a rental agreement. (4) 'Rental agreement' means any written or oral agreement, or lease, if any, between a landlord and tenant which establishes or modifies the terms, conditions, rules, or any other provisions concerning the use and occupancy of a dwelling unit. (5) 'Premises' means a dwelling unit and the structure of which it is a part and facilities and appurtenances therein and grounds, areas, and facilities for the use of tenants generally or whose use is promised to the tenant.
summary: Defines key terms for Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Part II of Chapter 83). Establishes definitions for dwelling unit (residential rental structures), landlord (owner/lessor), tenant (occupant under rental agreement), rental agreement (written or oral lease), and premises (dwelling unit and associated facilities).

title: Deposit money or advance rent; duty of landlord and tenant
text: 83.49 Deposit money or advance rent; duty of landlord and tenant.—(1) Whenever money is deposited or advanced by a tenant on a rental agreement as security for performance of the rental agreement or as advance rent for other than the next immediate rental period, the landlord or the landlord's agent shall either: (a) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate non-interest-bearing account in a Florida banking institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants. The landlord shall not commingle such money with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such money until such money is actually due to the landlord. (b) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate interest-bearing account in a Florida banking institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants, in which case the tenant shall receive and collect interest at least at 75 percent of the annualized average interest rate payable on such account or interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. (c) Post a surety bond in the circuit court in the county where the rental property is located, in the total amount of money held as security deposits or advance rent.
summary: Governs landlord's handling of security deposits and advance rent. Landlord must hold deposits in separate non-interest-bearing account, interest-bearing account (paying tenant 75% or 5% interest), or post surety bond. Prohibits commingling with landlord's funds. Establishes notice requirements and procedures for withholding deposits.

title: Service of notice of claim; time limitations
text: 558.004 Service of notice of claim; time limitations.—(1) A claimant shall serve written notice of claim on the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional at least 60 days before filing an action for damages or indemnity. (2) The notice must describe the claim in reasonable detail sufficient to determine the general nature of the defect. The notice must include a written statement that the claimant is providing this notice pursuant to this section and chapter and that the claimant is affording the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional an opportunity to inspect and the opportunity to make a written offer to repair or pay money as provided by s. 558.005. (3) Service of the notice of claim shall be by certified mail or delivery service at the last known address of the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional. (4) Strict compliance with the requirements of this section is not required. Substantial compliance with this section is sufficient to satisfy the requirements of this section.
summary: Requires claimants to provide 60-day pre-suit notice before filing construction defect actions. Notice must describe defect in reasonable detail and be served by certified mail. Substantial compliance is sufficient. Provides contractors opportunity to inspect and make repair/settlement offers before litigation.

title: Notice of claim; contents
text: 558.003 Notice of claim; contents.—The notice of claim required by s. 558.004 must state: (1) That the claimant asserts a construction defect claim against the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional. (2) The location of the claimed construction defects to the extent known by the claimant. (3) A description of the nature of the construction defects and the results of the defects to the extent known, including identification of the residential units or common areas affected. (4) A description of the damages to the extent known. (5) The names and addresses of the claimant and the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional against whom the claim is asserted.
summary: Specifies required contents of construction defect notice of claim. Must include assertion of defect claim, location of defects, nature and results of defects, description of damages, and names/addresses of parties. Provides contractors with sufficient detail to investigate and respond to claims.

title: Written response to notice of claim
text: 558.005 Written response to notice of claim.—(1) Within 30 days after receipt of the notice of claim, the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional may request, in writing, an opportunity to inspect the claimed construction defects. (2) Within 45 days after receipt of the written notice of claim or within 20 days after completion of the inspection, whichever occurs later, the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional shall serve on the claimant a written response by certified mail stating: (a) That the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional will make no offer; (b) That the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional disputes liability and will make no offer; (c) An offer to compromise and settle the claim; (d) An offer to inspect in accordance with subsection (1), if not previously made; or (e) An offer to remedy the construction defects at no cost to the claimant, with the proposed scope of the repair work or the amount of any monetary payment.
summary: Establishes contractor's response obligations after receiving construction defect notice. Contractor must respond within specified timeframes (30-45 days) stating: no offer, dispute of liability, settlement offer, inspection request, or repair offer. Provides structure for pre-litigation dispute resolution process.

title: Termination of tenancy without specific term
text: 83.57 Termination of tenancy without specific term.—(1) A tenancy without a specific duration, as defined in s. 83.46(2) or (3), may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56(4), as follows: (a) When the tenancy is from year to year, by giving not less than 60 days' notice prior to the end of any annual period; (b) When the tenancy is from quarter to quarter, by giving not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any quarterly period; (c) When the tenancy is from month to month, by giving not less than 15 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period; and (d) When the tenancy is from week to week, by giving not less than 7 days' notice prior to the end of any weekly period.
summary: Establishes notice requirements for terminating tenancies without specific terms (month-to-month, week-to-week, etc.). Notice periods vary by tenancy type: 60 days for year-to-year, 30 days for quarter-to-quarter, 15 days for month-to-month, 7 days for week-to-week. Written notice required.

title: Right of action for possession
text: 83.59 Right of action for possession.—If the rental agreement is terminated and the tenant does not vacate the premises, the landlord may recover possession of the dwelling unit as provided in this section. Notwithstanding any provision of the rental agreement to the contrary, however, the landlord's right to proceed under this section for the recovery of possession of a dwelling unit shall terminate if the tenant tenders to the landlord the full amount of rent due and any other moneys due under the rental agreement.
summary: Establishes landlord's right to pursue eviction action if tenant fails to vacate after termination of rental agreement. Landlord may recover possession through eviction proceedings. Tenant can cure and stop eviction by paying all rent and moneys due under the agreement.

title: Defenses to action for rent or possession
text: 83.60 Defenses to action for rent or possession.—(1) In an action for rent or possession, if the tenant interposes any defense other than payment, including the defense of a defective 3-day notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding. Failure to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry shall result in automatic dismissal of any defenses that the tenant may have to the action for eviction. (2) If the tenant asserts a defense to a landlord's action for possession under s. 83.51(1), the tenant shall assert all defenses and counterclaims arising out of the same transaction or occurrence in the eviction action.
summary: Governs tenant defenses in eviction proceedings. Tenant asserting defenses (except payment) must deposit rent into court registry to maintain defenses, or file motion to determine amount. Failure to pay rent into registry results in automatic dismissal of defenses. Requires assertion of all related defenses and counterclaims together.

title: Casualty damage
text: 83.63 Casualty damage.—If the premises are damaged or destroyed other than by the wrongful or negligent acts of the tenant so that the enjoyment of the premises is substantially impaired, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement and immediately vacate the premises. The tenant may vacate the part of the premises rendered unusable by the casualty, in which case the tenant's liability for rent shall be reduced by the fair rental value of that part of the premises damaged or destroyed. If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49(3) and return the security deposit and advance rent to the extent provided by s. 83.49(3)(a).
summary: Addresses tenant rights when rental property is damaged by casualty (fire, storm, etc.) not caused by tenant. Tenant may terminate lease and vacate if enjoyment substantially impaired, or may vacate damaged portion and receive rent reduction. Landlord must return security deposit if lease terminates.

title: Prohibited practices
text: 83.67 Prohibited practices.—A landlord of any dwelling unit governed by this part shall not cause, directly or indirectly, the termination or interruption of any utility service furnished the tenant, including, but not limited to, water, heat, light, electricity, gas, elevator, garbage collection, or refrigeration, whether or not the utility service is under the control of, or payment is made by, the landlord. A landlord who violates this section shall be liable to the tenant for actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees. This section shall not apply to a landlord who, pursuant to a court order, must discontinue a utility.
summary: Prohibits landlord from cutting off utilities (water, electricity, gas, etc.) to force tenant out. Landlord who violates faces liability for actual damages or 3 months' rent (whichever greater) plus attorney fees. Prohibition includes both direct and indirect utility shutoffs. Exception for court-ordered utility disconnection.

title: Foreclosure of real estate mortgages
text: 702.01 Foreclosure of real estate mortgages.—Any person having or holding a mortgage or lien upon real estate may foreclose the same in the manner provided for the foreclosure of mortgages generally. A foreclosure action may be brought by the mortgagee or any assignee, indorsee, or beneficiary thereof, and the plaintiff need not be in possession of the note or other instrument evidencing the indebtedness so long as the plaintiff has the right to enforce the note or instrument under the Uniform Commercial Code as adopted in this state.
summary: Establishes that mortgages and liens on real estate may be foreclosed through judicial foreclosure proceedings. Action may be brought by mortgagee or assignee. Plaintiff need not possess the note if they have the right to enforce it under the UCC. Sets foundation for foreclosure procedure.

title: Complaint; verification
text: 702.10 Complaint; verification.—The complaint in an action to foreclose a mortgage shall describe the note or other evidence of the debt secured by the mortgage, the mortgage, and the real property encumbered. The plaintiff or the plaintiff's representative or attorney shall verify by affidavit that the instrument on which the plaintiff's claim is based was not made for an illegal purpose. All other allegations of the complaint shall be verified by the plaintiff, the plaintiff's agent or attorney in accordance with s. 92.525(1)(b).
summary: Specifies required contents of foreclosure complaint. Must describe the note/debt, mortgage, and real property. Plaintiff or representative must verify by affidavit that the instrument was not made for illegal purpose. Complaint allegations must be verified per oath requirements.

title: Lis pendens
text: 702.11 Lis pendens.—No action to foreclose a mortgage on real property shall be valid as against any person not a party to the action or who has not otherwise been served with process in the action unless a notice of lis pendens has been recorded in accordance with s. 48.23, provided that if the property to be foreclosed consists of more than one parcel, an additional fee shall be required to record the notice of lis pendens only if one or more of such parcels are not contiguous.
summary: Requires recording of lis pendens (notice of pending litigation) in foreclosure actions to provide constructive notice to third parties. Without recorded lis pendens, foreclosure is not valid against persons not party to the action. Establishes notice requirement for foreclosure proceedings affecting real property.

title: Residential foreclosure mediation
text: 702.015 Residential foreclosure mediation.—(1) In any action to foreclose a residential property, if a homeowner files a motion to stay foreclosure proceedings for 120 days or such shorter period as is convenient to the parties and the court to allow the parties to mediate the case, and the homeowner has filed the motion within 30 days after service of the foreclosure complaint on the homeowner, the court shall enter an order staying the foreclosure proceedings for such period. (2) If the plaintiff in a residential foreclosure action has obtained a final judgment of foreclosure, and before the date of the foreclosure sale a homeowner requests mediation, the court may stay the sale and refer the case to mediation.
summary: Establishes residential foreclosure mediation program. Homeowners may request 120-day stay for mediation if motion filed within 30 days of service. Courts must grant stay if timely requested. Mediation may also be requested before foreclosure sale even after final judgment. Provides alternative resolution opportunity in residential foreclosures.

title: Limitations; general limitation
text: 95.011 Limitations; general limitation.—(1) Actions may be commenced as provided in this chapter. (2) Except as otherwise provided by law, an action for a legal or equitable claim shall be commenced within five years from the time the cause of action accrues. This subsection shall not apply to any action listed in s. 95.11. (3) A cause of action accrues when the last element constituting the cause of action occurs. (4) The running of the time within which an action must be commenced is tolled by the plaintiff's being absent from the state, but a nonresident plaintiff's absence shall not toll the running of the time.
summary: Establishes general 5-year statute of limitations for legal and equitable claims not specifically addressed in § 95.11. Defines when cause of action accrues (when last element occurs) and tolling provisions (plaintiff absence from state). Provides default limitation period for claims without specific limitation periods.

title: Limitations on actions for written contracts
text: 95.031 Limitations on actions for written contracts.—(1) A legal or equitable action on a contract, obligation, or liability founded on a written instrument shall be commenced within 5 years after the cause of action accrues, except as provided in s. 95.011 and except that an action for specific performance of a contract shall be commenced within 5 years. (2) When an action for specific performance of a contract to convey real property is commenced or may be commenced, and the Statute of Frauds requires that the contract be in writing, the action shall not be foreclosed by any statute of limitations until 5 years from the time that the statute begins to run against the party seeking specific performance or 5 years from the time that the party becomes entitled to specific performance, whichever time is later.
summary: Establishes 5-year statute of limitations for actions on written contracts. Covers legal and equitable actions on contracts, obligations, or liabilities founded on written instruments. Includes specific provision for specific performance actions for real property conveyances. Supersedes general limitation if applicable.

title: Short title
text: 501.201 Short title.—This part shall be cited as the 'Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.'
summary: Establishes the short title for Part II of Chapter 501 as the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act (FDUTPA). This statute is commonly cited in consumer protection cases throughout Florida.

title: Legislative declaration
text: 501.202 Legislative declaration.—It is the intent of the Legislature to protect the consuming public and legitimate business enterprises from those who engage in unfair methods of competition, or unconscionable, deceptive, or unfair acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce. These provisions shall be construed liberally to promote the purposes stated in this part.
summary: Declares legislative purpose of FDUTPA to protect consumers and legitimate businesses from unfair competition and deceptive practices. Statute must be construed liberally to promote consumer protection goals. Establishes public policy foundation for FDUTPA enforcement.

title: Definitions
text: 501.203 Definitions.—As used in this part, the term: (1) 'Person' means any natural person or his or her legal representative, partnership, corporation, company, trust, business entity, or association, and any agent, employee, salesperson, partner, officer, director, member, stockholder, associate, trustee, or cestui que trust thereof. (2) 'Trade or commerce' means the advertising, soliciting, providing, offering, or distributing, whether by sale, rental, or otherwise, of any good or service, or any property, whether tangible or intangible, or any other article, commodity, or thing of value, wherever situated. 'Trade or commerce' includes the conduct of any trade or commerce, however denominated, including any nonprofit or not-for-profit person or activity.
summary: Defines key terms for FDUTPA including 'person' (individuals, corporations, business entities, and their representatives) and 'trade or commerce' (broad definition encompassing advertising, selling, distributing goods/services, including nonprofit activities). Establishes broad applicability of consumer protection laws.

title: Lienable interests
text: 713.08 Lienable interests.—(1) Any person who improves real property and whose labor, services, or materials are not used beyond the site of such real property or buildings or improvements or fixtures, or site preparation of such real property, which includes the design or planning of the improvement, shall have a lien on such real property, buildings, or improvements, or fixtures. (2) The liens granted under this part shall only attach to the interest of the person who contracted for the improvements to the real property, including, but not limited to, the interest of the owner, and interests of coparceners, tenants in common, and joint tenants; and no lien claimed under this part shall attach to any interest in property held by a person who did not contract for such improvements and who properly posts a notice of nonresponsibility pursuant to s. 713.10.
summary: Defines lienable interests for mechanic's liens. Persons who improve real property through labor, services, or materials (including design/planning) have lien rights on the property. Liens attach only to interest of person who contracted for improvements, not to innocent owners who post notice of nonresponsibility.

title: Notice to owner
text: 713.16 Notice to owner.—(1) A lienor, other than a contractor, who is not in privity with the owner shall serve notice on the owner that he or she intends to look to the owner for payment. Unless the notice required by this section is served within 45 days of commencing to furnish labor, services, or materials, the lienor shall not have a lien on the real property for any labor, services, or materials furnished more than 45 days before service of the notice. (2) Service of the notice to owner may be made at any time during the progress of the work or thereafter, but not later than 45 days after the final furnishing of the labor, services, or materials by the lienor.
summary: Establishes notice to owner requirements for subcontractors and suppliers to preserve lien rights. Lienors not in privity with owner must serve notice within 45 days of starting work. Failure to timely serve notice results in loss of lien rights for work performed more than 45 days before service. Critical deadline for lien preservation.

title: Liens of laborers
text: 713.18 Liens of laborers.—Any person who performs labor on real property pursuant to a contract with the owner, a contractor under contract with the owner, or a subcontractor, shall have a lien on the real property upon which the labor is performed for the labor performed, unless the lienor is also a contractor or subcontractor. The lien for labor shall be in an amount based on the agreed compensation between the lienor and the party contracting with the lienor or, if no compensation is agreed upon, the reasonable value of the services.
summary: Grants mechanic's lien rights to laborers who perform work on real property. Lien amount based on agreed compensation or reasonable value if no agreement. Applies to labor performed pursuant to contract with owner, contractor, or subcontractor. Laborers have direct lien rights even without privity with owner.

title: Homeowner claims; process
text: 627.7011 Homeowner claims; process.—(1) An insurer is required to acknowledge receipt of a notice of a claim within 14 calendar days after receipt of such notice. (2) An insurer must begin an investigation of a claim within 7 calendar days after receiving a notice of claim. (3) An insurer must pay or deny a claim within 90 days after receipt of notice of the claim, unless the failure to pay is caused by factors beyond the control of the insurer which reasonably prevent such payment. If such factors exist, the insurer shall pay or deny the claim within 15 days after factors no longer prevent payment. If investigation of the claim remains incomplete, the insurer shall notify the policyholder in writing of the reasons the claim remains incomplete.
summary: Establishes strict timeframes for homeowner insurance claim processing in Florida. Insurer must acknowledge claim within 14 days, begin investigation within 7 days, and pay or deny within 90 days. If factors beyond control prevent payment, insurer must notify policyholder and resolve within 15 days after factors resolved.

title: Award of attorney's fees in civil actions
text: 57.041 Award of attorney's fees in civil actions.—Attorney's fees shall be awarded: (1) Pursuant to a written offer to settle a disputed claim for money damages as provided in this section. (2) The provisions of this section shall not apply to proposals made in eminent domain actions or family law matters. (3) In a civil action in which the relief sought is a money judgment, any party may serve upon an adverse party an offer to allow judgment to be taken against the party making the offer for the sum, or property, or to the effect therein specified, with costs then accrued. If the offer is accepted within 30 days after service, either party may then file the offer and notice of acceptance together with proof of service of the offer, and the clerk shall enter judgment. If the final judgment obtained by the offeree is at least 25 percent less favorable than such offer, and the offer complied with this subsection, the offeree must pay the offeror's reasonable costs, including investigative expenses, and attorney's fees incurred from the date the offer was served.
summary: Establishes offer of judgment procedures and attorney's fees consequences in civil money damages actions. Party may make written settlement offer; if rejected and offeree obtains judgment at least 25% less favorable than offer, offeree must pay offeror's costs and attorney fees from date of offer. Encourages reasonable settlement negotiations.

title: Misrepresentation in insurance applications
text: 627.701 Misrepresentation in insurance applications.—(1) No misrepresentation or false warranty made by the insured or in his or her behalf, in the negotiation of a contract of insurance or the application therefor, shall defeat or void the policy or prevent its attaching, unless: (a) The misrepresentation or false warranty is fraudulent or is material either to the acceptance of the risk or to the hazard assumed by the insurer; or (b) Had the true facts been made known to the insurer pursuant to the requirement of a complete application, the insurer in good faith would not have issued the policy or contract, or would not have issued it at the same premium rate, or would not have issued a policy or contract in as large an amount, or would not have provided coverage with respect to the hazard resulting in the loss.
summary: Limits insurer's ability to void coverage based on misrepresentations in insurance applications. Misrepresentation voids policy only if fraudulent, material to risk acceptance, or if insurer would not have issued policy/coverage had true facts been known. Protects insureds from policy rescission for immaterial misstatements.

title: Hurricane or windstorm insurance coverage
text: 627.7014 Hurricane or windstorm insurance coverage.—(1) A residential property insurance policy providing hurricane or windstorm coverage shall include a notice, in a separate section of the policy, which provides: 'NOTICE: This policy includes hurricane or windstorm coverage. The amount of coverage, deductibles, exclusions, and conditions may vary. You should review your policy carefully to determine the extent of your coverage.' (2) The notice must appear on the declarations page or on a page attached to the declarations page. (3) As used in this section, 'hurricane' means a storm system that the National Hurricane Center of the National Weather Service has declared to be a hurricane. (4) A homeowner's insurance policy that provides coverage against hurricanes or windstorms must include an offer of hurricane deductible options.
summary: Establishes notice requirements for residential property insurance policies providing hurricane or windstorm coverage. Requires conspicuous notice on declarations page alerting policyholder to hurricane coverage, deductibles, exclusions, and conditions. Mandates offer of hurricane deductible options. Critical for Florida hurricane coverage disputes.

title: Insurer's duty to acknowledge communications; investigations
text: 627.70131 Insurer's duty to acknowledge communications; investigations.—(1) Communications from insureds and claimants. — (a) Every insurer upon receiving notification of a claim or upon receipt of a request from a claimant for a copy of the insurance policy must, within 14 days of receipt of such notification or request, acknowledge receipt of such notice or request. The acknowledgment shall be in writing when sent by an insurer directly to a claimant who is not represented by legal counsel. (b) Every insurer, upon receiving any inquiry from the department directly related to a claim, must respond to such inquiry in writing within 20 days. (2) Every insurer must begin investigation of a claim immediately, but not more than 14 days after notification of an initial, reopened, or supplemental claim.
summary: Establishes insurer duties regarding communication acknowledgments and claim investigations. Insurer must acknowledge claims within 14 days, respond to department inquiries within 20 days, and begin investigation within 14 days of claim notification. Applies to initial, reopened, and supplemental claims. Foundation for bad faith insurance claims.

title: Action by state
text: 95.051 Action by state.—(1) An action to enforce any pecuniary penalty or forfeiture, whether given by a statute of this state or given by common law, or for a forfeiture of property under the laws of this state, if not specifically provided for in this chapter, shall be commenced within 5 years. (2) No statute of limitation shall be commenced or shall run in favor of any person against a claim by the state or an officer thereof authorized by law to sue on behalf of or for the benefit of the state.
summary: Establishes 5-year statute of limitations for state enforcement actions seeking penalties or forfeitures. Provides that no statute of limitations runs against claims by the state or its authorized officers. Sovereign immunity from limitations periods protects state's ability to enforce laws and collect debts without time bar.

title: Remedies for breach by buyer
text: 672.316 Remedies for breach by buyer.—(1) Unless otherwise agreed or unless the circumstances indicate the contrary, the seller on discovering the buyer's breach may: (a) Withhold delivery of such goods; (b) Stop delivery by any bailee as hereafter provided (s. 672.705); (c) Proceed under the next section respecting goods still unidentified to the contract; (d) Resell and recover damages as hereafter provided (s. 672.706); (e) Recover damages for nonacceptance (s. 672.708) or in a proper case the price (s. 672.709); (f) Cancel. (2) Where the seller has made a substantial beginning of the manufacture of unfinished goods or procurement of materials and the manufacture or procurement is reasonably suited only to the contract and the buyer breaches, the seller may complete the manufacture or procurement and identify the goods to the contract or cease the manufacture or procurement and resell for scrap or salvage value.
summary: Establishes seller's remedies under the UCC when buyer breaches a sales contract. Seller may withhold delivery, stop delivery, resell goods and recover damages, recover damages for non-acceptance, recover the contract price, or cancel. If buyer breaches during manufacturing, seller may complete or cease manufacturing. Provides comprehensive remedies for breach of sale of goods contracts.

title: Landlord's access to dwelling unit
text: 83.53 Landlord's access to dwelling unit.—(1) The tenant shall not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord to enter the dwelling unit from time to time in order to inspect the premises, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, supply agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen, or contractors. (2) The landlord may enter the dwelling unit at any time for the protection or preservation of the premises. The landlord may enter the dwelling unit upon reasonable notice to the tenant and at a reasonable time for the purpose of repair of the premises. 'Reasonable notice' for the purpose of repair is notice given at least 12 hours prior to the entry, and reasonable time for the purpose of repair shall be between the hours of 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. The landlord may enter the dwelling unit when necessary for the further purposes set forth in subsection (1) under any of the following circumstances: (a) With the consent of the tenant; (b) In case of emergency; (c) When the tenant unreasonably withholds consent; or (d) If the tenant is absent from the premises for a period of time equal to one-half the time for periodic rental payments.
summary: Limits landlord's right to enter rental property. Requires 12-hour advance notice for non-emergency entry between 7:30 AM and 8:00 PM. Exceptions include emergencies, tenant consent, or when tenant unreasonably withholds consent. Protects tenant's privacy and quiet enjoyment while allowing landlord reasonable access for repairs and showings.

title: Retaliatory conduct
text: 83.64 Retaliatory conduct.—(1) It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant. In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith. Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where: (a) The tenant has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises; (b) The tenant has organized, encouraged, or participated in a tenants' organization; (c) The tenant has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56(1); (d) The tenant is a servicemember who has terminated a rental agreement pursuant to s. 83.682; (e) The tenant has paid rent to a condominium, cooperative, or homeowners' association after demand for payment by the association pursuant to s. 83.67(4). (2) Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession. (3) In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause. Examples of good cause include, but are not limited to, good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules, or violation of the terms of this chapter.
summary: Prohibits landlords from retaliating against tenants who exercise their rights, such as filing complaints with governmental agencies, joining tenant organizations, or withholding rent for valid reasons. Creates presumption of retaliation if adverse action taken within 6 months. Landlord can rebut by proving legitimate reason such as nonpayment or lease violations. Essential tenant protection statute.

title: Comparative fault
text: 768.81 Comparative fault.—(1) APPLICABILITY.—This section applies to any action arising after the effective date of this act based on negligence and to any action based on strict liability for products liability. (2) EFFECT OF CONTRIBUTORY FAULT.—In an action to which this section applies, any contributory fault chargeable to the claimant diminishes proportionately the amount awarded as economic and noneconomic damages for an injury attributable to the claimant's contributory fault, but does not bar recovery. This rule applies even though the fault of the claimant may be equal to or greater than the fault of all others; however, if a claimant's fault is greater than the combined fault of all defendants, recovery by the claimant in the action shall be barred. (3) DETERMINATION OF PERCENTAGES OF FAULT.—In determining the percentages of fault, the trier of fact shall consider both the nature of the conduct of each party at fault and the extent of the causal relation between the conduct and the damages claimed. (4) APPLICABILITY TO COMPARATIVE NEGLIGENCE.—The principles of subsection (2) shall also apply to strict liability claims.
summary: Establishes Florida's modified comparative fault rule. Plaintiff can recover damages reduced by their percentage of fault unless plaintiff is more than 50% at fault, in which case recovery is barred. Applies to negligence and strict liability claims. Jury determines each party's percentage of fault based on conduct and causation. Essential statute for all personal injury cases including car accidents, slip & fall, premises liability, and product liability.

title: Punitive damages; limitation; exception
text: 768.73 Punitive damages; limitation; exception.—(1)(a) In any civil action, no claim for punitive damages shall be permitted unless there is a reasonable showing by evidence in the record or proffered by the claimant which would provide a reasonable basis for recovery of such damages. The claimant may move to amend her or his complaint to assert a claim for punitive damages as allowed by the rules of civil procedure. The rules of civil procedure shall be liberally construed so as to allow the claimant discovery of evidence which appears reasonably calculated to lead to admissible evidence on the issue of punitive damages. (b) A defendant may be held liable for punitive damages only if the trier of fact, based on clear and convincing evidence, finds that the defendant was personally guilty of intentional misconduct or gross negligence. (2) The trier of fact may consider the following factors in determining whether to assess punitive damages and the amount of such damages: (a) The severity of the harm or potential harm caused by the defendant's conduct; (b) The duration of the conduct; (c) The defendant's awareness of the wrongfulness or probable consequences of the conduct; (d) Any efforts by the defendant to mitigate the effects of the conduct; (e) The financial resources and income of the defendant; (f) Other punitive damage awards against the defendant for the same conduct.
summary: Governs punitive damages in Florida civil actions. Requires clear and convincing evidence of intentional misconduct or gross negligence. Caps punitive damages at 3x compensatory damages (or $500,000 minimum). Lists factors jury must consider including severity of harm, duration, defendant's awareness, and financial resources. Motion to amend complaint required to assert punitive damages claim.

title: Exemplary damages; evidence of profits
text: 768.76 Exemplary damages; evidence of profits.—(1) Where exemplary damages are claimed by a party, that party may introduce evidence of the profits of the opposing party for the purpose of proving the amount of exemplary damages. (2) In any case in which exemplary damages are claimed, the following evidence is admissible at trial if otherwise admissible under the Florida Evidence Code: (a) Evidence of a party's profits; (b) Evidence of a party's wealth; and (c) Evidence of a party's financial condition. (3) This section does not limit the other types of evidence that may be considered relevant in proving the amount of exemplary damages.
summary: Allows admission of defendant's profits, wealth, and financial condition as evidence when exemplary (punitive) damages are claimed. Complements § 768.73 by specifying what financial evidence is admissible. Important for proving appropriate punitive damage amounts based on defendant's ability to pay and deterrence goals.

title: Valued policy law
text: 627.702 Valued policy law.—(1) If a policy of insurance, other than a liability or marine insurance policy, is issued or delivered in this state, and if the real or personal property that is insured is wholly destroyed, without criminal fault on the part of the insured or the insured's assigns, the insurer, except as provided in subsection (2), shall be liable for the full amount specified in the policy, without regard to the actual value of the insured property at the time of the loss. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply: (a) To marine insurance; (b) To property in which the insured has less than 100 percent ownership interest; (c) To a policy that provides for a stated amount to be paid in the event of total loss, whether or not that is the only stated amount in the policy; (d) To property if the insured has underinsured the property; or (e) To any payment under a policy that is less than 80 percent of the replacement cost of the insured property. (3) For the purpose of this section, if the building on the insured premises is wholly destroyed by a covered peril, it shall be considered a total loss even if a portion of the foundation remains and can be used in reconstruction.
summary: Florida's valued policy law requires insurers to pay full policy limits for total losses without proving actual cash value. Applies when property is completely destroyed by covered peril without criminal fault. Exceptions for marine insurance, partial ownership, and underinsured property. Critical Florida-specific insurance statute for property damage claims, especially hurricane and fire total losses.

title: Attorney's fees
text: 627.428 Attorney's fees.—(1) Upon the rendition of a judgment or decree by any of the courts of this state against an insurer and in favor of any named or omnibus insured or the named beneficiary under a policy or contract executed by the insurer, the trial court or, in the event of an appeal in which the insured or beneficiary prevails, the appellate court shall adjudge or decree against the insurer and in favor of the insured or beneficiary a reasonable sum as fees or compensation for the insured's or beneficiary's attorney prosecuting the suit in which the recovery is had. (2) If the insurer tenders the liability limits and the claimant rejects the tender and if the judgment exceeds the tender, the court shall adjudge or decree attorney's fees against the insurer and in favor of the prevailing party in an amount based upon the entire judgment. (3) This section applies to any judgment or decree entered in favor of an insured or a beneficiary, even when such judgment or decree is not based upon the terms of the policy or contract, which arises out of any matter relating to the policy or contract, including, but not limited to, any right or benefit provided for under the policy or contract and any tort, contract, or bad faith claim brought by an insured or beneficiary against the insurer.
summary: Mandates attorney's fees for insureds who prevail in lawsuits against insurers, including policy disputes, bad faith claims, and breach of contract. Fees awarded even if judgment not based on policy terms if claim relates to policy. If insurer tenders limits but claimant prevails for more, fees based on entire judgment. Critical fee-shifting statute that levels playing field against insurers and encourages settlement.

title: Substitute for security deposits
text: 83.62 Substitute for security deposits.—(1) In lieu of the security deposit required by s. 83.49, a landlord may accept a surety bond, executed by the tenant as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in this state, in an amount equal to the security deposit which would otherwise be required. (2) If the landlord accepts such surety bond, the landlord shall return any security deposit received and pay any interest due thereon to the tenant within 30 days. (3) The surety bond shall provide that the surety shall indemnify the landlord for all losses and damages as set forth in s. 83.49, up to the amount of the bond. (4) The surety bond shall be for a term of at least 1 year and shall be renewed annually during the term of the tenancy. (5) The tenant shall be responsible for all costs and premiums associated with the surety bond.
summary: Allows tenants to provide a surety bond instead of a cash security deposit. Surety bond must equal the deposit amount and be renewed annually. If landlord accepts bond, any cash deposit must be returned within 30 days. Bond indemnifies landlord for damages up to bond amount. Tenant pays all bond costs. Alternative to traditional security deposit for tenants who prefer not to tie up cash.

title: Notice of contest of lien; discharge of lien
text: 713.20 Notice of contest of lien; discharge of lien.—(1) An owner of property subject to a claim of lien may contest such lien by recording a notice of contest in the same office in which the claim of lien was recorded. The notice of contest must identify the claim of lien being contested by identifying the names of the parties, the date of recording, and the official records book and page or instrument number of the claim of lien. (2) The lienor must file suit to enforce the lien within 60 days after the service of the notice of contest or the claim of lien shall be deemed abandoned and shall be discharged of record by the clerk. (3) In lieu of recording a notice of contest, the owner may obtain a discharge of the lien by filing with the clerk a surety bond in an amount equal to one and one-half times the amount of the claim of lien, or by depositing with the clerk cash or a cashier's check in an amount equal to one and one-half times the amount of the claim of lien. (4) Upon the filing of such bond or deposit, the clerk shall issue a certificate discharging the lien from the property, and the lien shall attach to the bond or deposit.
summary: Establishes procedure for property owners to contest mechanic's liens by recording notice of contest. After service of notice, lienor must file foreclosure suit within 60 days or lien is abandoned. Alternatively, owner can discharge lien by posting bond or deposit equal to 1.5x the lien amount. Critical statute for lien dispute resolution and establishing deadlines for enforcement actions.

title: Enforcement by Department of Legal Affairs
text: 501.2105 Enforcement by Department of Legal Affairs.—(1) The Department of Legal Affairs may bring an action to obtain a declaratory judgment that an act or practice violates this part, to enjoin any person who is violating or is about to violate this part, or to obtain restitution of property or other relief as may be appropriate. (2) In any action brought by the Department of Legal Affairs, if the court finds a violation of this part, the court shall enjoin the act or practice and impose a civil penalty of not more than $10,000 for each violation. For a willful violation, the court may impose a civil penalty of not more than $15,000 per violation. If the court finds that a violation affects one or more elderly persons or handicapped persons, the court may treble the amount of the civil penalty. (3) The state attorney of any judicial circuit in which an unlawful act or practice occurs may bring a civil action in the name of the state for declaratory judgment, temporary or permanent injunction, restitution of property, or civil penalty. (4) In determining the amount of a civil penalty, the court shall consider: the degree of harm to the consuming public, the duration of the violation, the assets and income of the violator, and other factors deemed relevant by the court.
summary: Authorizes Florida Department of Legal Affairs and state attorneys to enforce FDUTPA through civil actions. Allows declaratory judgments, injunctions, restitution, and civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation ($15,000 if willful). Penalties may be trebled if violation affects elderly or handicapped persons. Court considers harm, duration, and violator's financial condition. Public enforcement mechanism for consumer protection.

title: Inspection rights
text: 558.006 Inspection rights.—(1) Upon receipt of the notice of claim required by s. 558.004, the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional and his or her representatives are entitled to inspect the property alleged to contain a construction defect and all relevant plans, specifications, and other documents. (2) The claimant shall provide access to the claimant's property and documents for inspection by the contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional within 14 days after receipt of a written request for inspection, unless the parties agree to a different schedule. (3) The inspection may be scheduled during normal business hours or at any other mutually agreeable time. (4) The contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional shall be permitted to conduct reasonable and customary destructive testing as is necessary to fully and completely evaluate the nature, extent, and cause of the alleged construction defect, provided that the claimant receives reasonable advance notice and the contractor agrees to restore the property to its pre-testing condition. (5) If the claimant fails to provide reasonable access to the property or documents, the claimant shall not be entitled to recover from such contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or design professional any costs or fees incurred in investigating, repairing, or litigating the construction defect.
summary: Grants contractors and other construction professionals the right to inspect property and documents after receiving notice of construction defect claim. Claimant must provide access within 14 days. Allows reasonable destructive testing with advance notice and obligation to restore. Failure to provide access bars recovery of investigation, repair, and litigation costs. Critical for pre-suit investigation and dispute resolution in construction defect cases.
